Claim C7 has no evidence linked to it: "Application of a neural network to optimize acute care with a predictive model has not so far been reported in the literature."

The paper says hyper-parameters were optimized 'based on performance in the training and the validation sets' and that lambda 0.02 was chosen 'to minimize error on the validation set'. The validation set is also the set on which the reported performance (Table 2) is measured, so the reported validation metrics are not from a set held out from model selection. The paper does not report how many configurations were tried.

Accuracy is defined twice differently: p.32370 'Accuracy, defined as percentage of delay > 45 min correctly predicted' (which reads as recall of the positive class) and Table 2 'Correctly predicted / Total'. The reported 60% equals the overall accuracy (36/60 in the stored output), not the recall (66%).

The validation set has 34 positives and 27 negatives (test_data.csv). Predicting the majority class (delay >45 min) for every case gives accuracy 34/61 = 55.7% (33/60 = 55.0% in the stored 60-row run). The reported 60% is 4.3 points above this no-information baseline; no baseline model (majority class, logistic regression) is reported in the paper.

No confidence interval or uncertainty is reported for any of the four validation metrics, and the validation set has 61 cases (60 in the stored run). With 61 cases a 95% Wilson interval for accuracy 60% spans roughly 47-72%, which includes the majority-class baseline.

The paper states a temporal split (2003-2017 training, last 2 years validation) but the released data are two csv files with no dates or case identifiers, so the split cannot be verified from the materials; the code simply reads the two files.

The paper reports a single training run at learning rate 0.15 and does not state a random seed or report run-to-run variation. The code sets xavier_initializer(seed=1) per variable but no graph-level seed, so repeated runs differ.

'Application of neural network in this context of optimizing acute care based on a predictive model has not so far been reported in literature.' No search strategy or citation supports this novelty statement, and the paper cites only four references.

With the paper's own choices the claim 'The network reaches at least 60% accuracy and at least 63% precision on the validation set' does not hold on re-run (effect = 0.6557377049180317). [Yellow, not red (build_passport.py): only our own re-run disagrees with the paper; red needs two sources that conflict.]
